newsitem.title: ISRAEL: FEATURE-Life on the Arab-Israeli divide in Hebron.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Life on the Arab-Israeli divide in Hebron.

text.p: When darkness creeps along the wall dividing Arab and Jew in Hebron, the Dana children move indoors.
Fear of Jewish settlers drives them from their own backyard to spend evenings behind metal-shuttered windows. Settlers have hurled stones, bottles and abuse at the Dana families for years.

One teenage daughter is too afraid to venture into the kitchen at the back of the house at night to make coffee for her parents. The toddlers have nightmares. The older kids don't sleep well. Their grades at school are slipping. An Israeli psychiatrist has said they are all traumatised.
It wasn't supposed to be like this. The Dana brothers, Shaker and Niman, built their homes side by side in the 1970s, confident that this Hebron hill would be the bedrock of a new family dynasty.
But at the bottom of their garden is a fence belonging to Kiryat Arba, one of the most militant settlements in the West Bank.
"Unfortunately," says Shaker, a father of 12 who looks older than his 45 years, "We have them as neighbours. They want us off this land."
The two Palestinian brothers have a 20-year-long litany of complaints of violence and harassment against their armed neigbours culminating in an apparent arson attack this November.
"My son was sleeping here," said Niman, pointing to a charred corner beneath a kitchen window. "He heard breaking glass and came to my room saying settlers were trying to break in."
"I rushed down and when I opened the door I saw an explosion and suddenly the whole room was in flames," Niman said.
The family escaped serious injury although one child spent 12 days in hospital after inhaling smoke.
SETTLERS SEEN IN AREA
The Dana families and several neighbours say they saw settlers in the area before the fire broke out, simultaneously at opposite ends of a large room beneath broken windows.
Settler spokesman Noam Arnon said: "I don't believe that Jews did it."
Niman is in no doubt who torched half his home. He fingered settlers but says he does not expect that the Israeli police will do much about it.
"They never have in the past," chips in his brother Shaker, who has sheaves of complaints filed against the settlers for stoning and shooting incidents over the years.
"We reported the fire but police have still not come back to us to tell us who did it," Shaker Dana said.
"This has been the pattern whenever they throw stones. They have shot holes with live bullets into my water tanks and once they threw a percussion grenade into this room," he said.

"The police have come and done nothing." Shaker has built a two-metre (six-foot) high wall between him and the settlement fence, and has put metal grills and shutters on his windows, saying they are better protection than the police.
Shaker Dana is well known to the police, who say they investigate his complaints.
But a year ago in frustration he turned to Israeli human rights lawyer Lynda Bryer. She filed a petition in the Israeli High Court demanding police action. She is still waiting for a hearing.

"The police and judicial authorities are in collaboration," Bryer said. "If we are waiting for a hearing since the 19th of November (1995) and the story is screaming, really screaming. I want to ask you what that means other than collaboration."
"APARTHEID SYSTEM"
Bryer, a native South African, adds: "This, by the way, is the worse kind of racism...it's the real apartheid system, where the authorities will not (intervene)."
Palestinians still under Israeli control in Hebron have nobody to turn to when harassed by settlers, she says.
"There is no such thing as civil authorities for Palestinians," Bryer said.
She accuses the settlers of wanting to clear the Danas off their land in order to expand the settlement, a charge denied by Tsuriel Popovich, spokesman for Kiryat Arba municipality.
"We know of no such plans," Popovich said.
The Dana brothers said they were both offered inflated prices for their property years ago but refused. Now they make it a point of honour to stay put.
Popovich said the Danas' complaints were old.

"If there were such things, there was a period when some of the children were throwing stones, when this became known the municipality spoke with the parents and there was a whole business with the school and they spoke to kids about how this is not they way we do things," Popovich said. He denied charges of systematic harassment.
"If these are all just kids," retorts Shaker, "Why do some of them have beards and guns?"
VOLCANO WAITING TO EXPLODE
Israeli psychiatrist Moshe Landesman says in a report on Shaker Dana's household that the family is a volcano waiting to explode.

"The children here need to get away, they are suffering from typical trauma reaction, itching, shaking, recurrent nightmares, they replay trauma in games," Landesman writes in the report shown by Shaker.
"We did not make this up," Shaker says, brandishing the report. "We are not suffering because just a few children threw stones over the fence," Shaker said.
Despite his anger Shaker was in hospitable mood. His wife had just given birth in the next room of their sparsely furnished home to their 12th child.
"I'm not waging this fight for myself. Our lives have been ruined. I'm doing it for them, the children," he said.

Yet neither he nor his brother thinks things will improve substantially, even if Israel and the PLO resolve their differences and Israeli troops leave 80 percent of Hebron under the stalled Palestinian self-rule deal.
"Kiryat Arba will still be there. How can we live next to such people in peace?" Shaker asked, echoing a question heard on the other side of the divide.
